title: Recapitulation
hook: Irenaeus: Christ lives every stage of human life again, rightly, to heal it

segments.voice: Yesterday, moral influence: a centurion who watched how someone loved and changed. Your line was love that changes us. What reaction did love change? Day one thousand eighty-six.

A baby who has to be fed. A boy who stays behind in the city and leaves his parents searching. A man the neighbors know as the carpenter. A grown man with friends, and enemies, and a job to finish. That list is Jesus, and it's also a list of stages a human life can pass through. Luke's Gospel even pauses on the in-between years with one line: "And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man." He grew. He didn't arrive finished. An early Christian bishop named Irenaeus saw something in that. He thought those ordinary stages weren't a detour on the way to the cross. They were part of the rescue. Today's word: recapitulation.
screen: `THE STAGES ARE PART OF THE RESCUE.`

segments.voice: Recapitulation means going over it again, from the top. Irenaeus was a bishop in Gaul, in what is now France, and he found the idea in a line in Paul's letter to the Ephesians: God's plan is to "gather together in one all things in Christ." Here's how he heard it. The human story went wrong at its head, with Adam. So Christ comes as a new head and lives the human story over again, this time rightly. Paul puts the two side by side: "For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive." And to the Romans: "For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous." Irenaeus loved the matching details. A disobedience at a tree in the garden; an obedience on a tree outside Jerusalem. Eve tied a knot by her disobedience; he pictured Mary untying it by her obedience, her yes. And he went through the ages of life. Christ became an infant, he wrote, to make infants holy; a child for children; a young man for the young. Each stage, in Irenaeus's telling, he passed through, and lived it whole. So in this picture the cross isn't the only place where saving happens. The manger is too. The workbench is too. The hungry days in the desert are too. The cross and the empty tomb finish it. Like a song played again from the top: the same tune, but this time every note true. That's what this word means: the human story, lived again, and healed from the inside.
screen: `GOING OVER IT AGAIN, FROM THE TOP.`
`IN ADAM ALL DIE, IN CHRIST ALL ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring your own stage of life into the light. Settle, and breathe. Ask where you are right now. Starting out. In the thick of it. Raising someone. Caring for someone. Slowing down. Starting over. Name it simply. Then ask what this stage is asking of you right now. Patience, maybe. Courage. Letting go. Let one answer come, and stay with it. If you pray, you can pray for your own stage of life, as one Christ has walked. If you don't, just let this stage be seen, all of it. The bell holds the time.
Recapitulation. Going over it again from the top: Irenaeus's picture of Christ living each stage of human life rightly, to heal it.
Your line: every age healed. Today, be kind to someone at a different stage than yours: a child, a teenager, someone much older. Day one thousand eighty-six.

howItsDone: Christians who follow the church year walk through Christ's life each year, from his birth at Christmas through his childhood, ministry, death and resurrection, and Irenaeus is honored as a saint in Catholic and Orthodox churches.

notes: Irenaeus as bishop of Lyon in Gaul ('in what is now France'): standard; confirm under the claims rule.
Recapitulation ages passage (infant, child, youth) is Against Heresies 2.22.4; Eve's knot and Mary untying it is 3.22.4; the tree and the tree is 5.16.3 / 5.19.1. Paraphrased; confirm refs.
'Recapitulation means going over it again, from the top' is a gloss on the English/Latin word, not an etymology claim; confirm acceptable.
Irenaeus's link to Ephesians 1:10 is standard; the Greek ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι is the verb in that verse. Confirm spelling and pronunciation.
Hook's 'a young man learning a trade' rests on Mark 6:3 ('the carpenter'); the 'workbench' in the teach too. Confirm.
The 'song played again in tune' image is the writer's, not Irenaeus's.
Irenaeus is commemorated by Catholic and Orthodox churches (and some others); howItsDone names two. Confirm.

Editor pass: hook no longer says the boy Jesus 'gets lost' (Luke 2: he stayed behind and his parents searched) or that he was 'learning a trade' (Mark 6:3 says only 'the carpenter'); 'stages everybody passes through' softened; 'he took the idea from' Ephesians softened to 'found the idea in'; 'every stage we live, he lived first' corrected to Irenaeus's 'passed through'; practice changed from naming one hard and one good thing and holding both (day 1081's practice) to asking what this stage asks of you; howItsDone no longer says the church year walks through Christ's 'whole' life; lowercased the word in the hook.

Audit pass (2026-10-02): Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.22.4) pairs Eve's disobedience with Mary's obedience; Genesis never has Eve 'saying no', so the teach and match pair now say disobedience. Fixed the self-contradictory song image ('every bar the same, but in tune'). Myth item 'took his big idea from Ephesians' softened to match the teach.
